data.text/html:
YouTube monetization signals by country

In November 2023 YouTube removed the public flag that said whether a channel is monetized. Unless you own the channel, you can now only infer it from what the channel shows in public. This open dataset did that for 3,080 trending channels in 50 countries in September 2026. The question here is narrow: how much of the gap between countries survives once you account for small samples and for the channels that couldn't be classified?

Share of channels with the signals, with 95% intervals

Dot = share of the channels checked in that country. Line = 95% Wilson interval. The number after each country is how many channels were checked. Click a dot (shift-click for more) to pull its row into the table below.

data.text/markdown: How to read it. With about 60 channels per country, the median interval is 22 percentage points wide. Taiwan comes out on top at 48%, but 30 of the other 49 countries shown have intervals that reach into its interval. Countries a few points apart can't be told apart with samples this size, so compare the intervals, not just the dots. Where you draw the line matters as much. Switch to "Likely or possibly monetized" and the order changes a lot. Tanzania has no channels in "likely" but 48 of 60 in "possibly", which puts it in the top third on the wider measure. Nigeria goes from 10 of 60 to 52 of 60. The interval only covers sampling noise. It treats the channels in a country as a random draw from a larger group of similar channels and says nothing about how the channels were picked in the first place (see the notes at the bottom).

data.text/html:
The full verdict mix

Each checked channel got one of four verdicts. Same country order as above. Gray is the share that couldn't be classified.

What the unclassified channels could do

The gray bar runs from "none of the unclassified channels qualify" to "all of them do". The dot is the share among classified channels, which is what you get if the unclassified ones split the same way as the rest. In Sri Lanka, 25 of 60 channels came back "unable to determine", so its share could sit anywhere from 8% to 50%.

data.text/markdown:
About the data

Source. YouTube monetization signals by country, September 2026 snapshot, published by MonetizationKit under CC BY 4.0 (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23401599). The notebook reads the CSV from the dataset's GitHub repository, supertj/youtube-monetization-by-country. What a verdict means. Each channel was checked once against public signals of being in the YouTube Partner Program and put in one of four groups: likely monetized, possibly monetized, likely not, or unable to determine. A verdict is an inference from what the channel shows in public, not a statement from YouTube. Which channels. The channels behind each region's most popular videos, pulled from the YouTube Data API across 111 regions and 10 categories, then filled toward a target number per country. These are trending channels, most with hundreds of thousands of subscribers. A low share for a country means the big channels checked there showed fewer signals. It is not that country's monetization rate. Counts. The 50 published rows add up to 3,080 channels. The dataset's README gives 3,192 channels checked overall; countries with fewer than 30 checked channels are not published. The live page reads differently. MonetizationKit keeps a live version of this table that is recomputed weekly. It mixes in channels people looked up on the site, and it uses scoring rules revised in late September and early October 2026, with older checks re-scored, so its "likely" shares are higher than in this snapshot. Use one or the other. Don't mix rows from the two.
